stages.title: Foundations: a learnable skill, calm enough to connect
stages.purpose: Replace the belief that communication is a fixed talent with a practice mindset, give tools to manage nerves, and establish that every communication starts with audience and purpose.
stages.rationale: Perfectionism and unmanaged anxiety undermine every later skill, so they come first: the mastery frame and connection over perfection, then calming the body, knowing that nerves are far less visible than they feel (illusion of transparency), relabeling arousal, reframing the moment, and acting before feeling ready. For persistent fear, structured practice programs have the strongest evidence (Ebrahimi, High). The stage ends by pointing attention outward to audience and purpose (AIM, stay on course), which the listening stage builds on.

stages.title: Listening and understanding others
stages.purpose: Build full, visible attention; correct overconfidence in reading people; teach looping; diagnose what kind of conversation the other person is having.
stages.rationale: Attention is the High-confidence base, and the listening meta-analysis shows why it pays: feeling heard goes with trust and liking more than almost anything else. Attention is then made visible and aimed at the bottom line. Humility about reading people (including the research that lies and inner states cannot be read from body language) motivates perspective getting and looping as verification, and inquiry before advice. Empathy's three skills and the three realities give a model of intent versus impact that feedback needs later. The three kinds of conversations and matching turn listening into choosing a response, which Stage 3 requires.

stages.title: Conversation and connection
stages.purpose: Move from small talk to real connection through questions, topic management, depth, reciprocal disclosure, levity, appreciation, everyday responsiveness, staying in touch and good endings.
stages.rationale: TALK provides the map. Curiosity and follow-ups are the easiest high-return change and boomerasking the most common failure. Topic preparation and the pyramid show how to climb; the depth evidence, the liking gap and deep questions justify climbing. Disclosure follows because depth is reciprocal (pace, vulnerability, dropping image management). Levity with a safety check, turning toward everyday bids, appreciation, responding actively to good news and reaching out to lapsed ties extend connection into friendships, family and partners. Knowing when to end completes the stage. Trust built here is what Stage 6 relies on.

stages.title: Clarity and structure in speech and writing
stages.purpose: Make messages easy to understand: beat the curse of knowledge, lead with the core, use a reusable structure, make it concrete, and adapt for busy readers, text and async work.
stages.rationale: The curse of knowledge explains why clarity is hard and extends AIM from Stage 1; asking listeners for their version catches the misunderstandings speakers miss. Focus and the core decide what to say, parachuting in where to start, the pyramid how to order support, and What So What Now What the shape. Concreteness, analogies and human-scale numbers make it land. The written block applies this to text: ABC editing, cutting whole ideas and limiting each message to one easy ask for busy readers, the tone check because senders overestimate how well tone comes across, pause-verify-iterate, stating your response clock for async work, and extra warmth online. Clarity must precede persuasion.

stages.title: Influence and memorable messages
stages.purpose: Move people to act by leading with their benefit, using persuasive structures, making ideas stick, building credibility and reciprocity, working with identity and values, and reducing resistance instead of pushing harder.
stages.rationale: Benefit-first persuasion extends audience thinking. Structures come before stickiness so the reader has a skeleton to strengthen. SUCCESs organizes the stickiness tools (unexpected, curiosity, stories with transportation research on what makes them work, a light line). Credibility, reciprocity and the exchange model for influence without authority follow, then emotional spread. Identity and moral reframing explain why good arguments fail, and the stage closes with the best-evidenced ways through resistance: drawing out the other person's own reasons (motivational interviewing) and exchanging stories rather than arguments. These bridge into difficult conversations.

stages.title: Difficult situations
stages.purpose: Handle feedback, speaking up, conflict, bad news, apologies, saying no, boundaries and distress without damaging the relationship.
stages.rationale: Receiving feedback comes first because it is the reader's own side and shows why others' data matters. Raising pinches early sets timing, and the voice research (will it matter, is it safe) explains why people stay silent with those above them. Real feelings, behavior plus impact and behavior-not-personality build the message; the 4 I's packages it; problem solving sets the stance. Conflict moves from diagnosis (find the layer) to the couples research on what predicts escalation (the four horsemen) and when directness helps, then regulation, receptiveness and group norms. Delivering bad news (SPIKES) follows preparation for the hardest conversations. Apologies, with research on which parts matter most, lead into repair. Saying no (the positive no, and evidence that declines sting less than feared) and boundaries follow, and supporting distress closes the stage with the comfort ladder and presence over fixing, drawing on all earlier skills, including looping from Stage 2.

stages.title: Mastery: groups, high stakes, and deliberate practice
stages.purpose: Integrate skills under pressure, in meetings, negotiations and in front of groups, lead conversations that elevate others, and install a lasting practice loop.
stages.rationale: The six-step method recaps Stages 1, 2 and 4 as one sequence for on-the-spot speaking; ADD, restating the question so relevance is visible, prompts instead of scripts and the toast apply it. Delivery follows once content is in place (contested elements flagged; vocal confidence amplifies but does not replace a strong case). Group leadership extends Stage 3 to teams, and meeting science turns it into design: before, during and after, silent idea generation, and reducing video fatigue. Negotiation integrates listening, structure and influence under high stakes: interests over positions, testing the fixed-pie assumption, and knowing your BATNA (which also backs a firm no). The canvas is the high-stakes integration of AIM, and the guide ends with video review and coaching so learning continues.

convergent_concepts.concept: Outward attention beats self-monitoring
convergent_concepts.agreement: Self-focused attention blocks listening and fluent speech; attending to the other person improves the interaction and lowers anxiety.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Madson treats attention as contemplative practice; David Brooks stresses making attention visible; Abrahams frames it as a pressure skill that also buys time; Schramm applies it to presenting; Duhigg's neural framing is flagged as overreach.

convergent_concepts.concept: Ask more questions, especially follow-ups
convergent_concepts.agreement: People ask too few questions; follow-ups signal listening and increase liking; do not use questions as a launch pad for yourself.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Wood Brooks gives a four-type taxonomy and warns about too many switches; Duhigg focuses on groups; Connect favors open how and what questions and avoiding why; Abrahams frames it as being interested, not interesting. The main study is modest, critiqued by Kluger and Malloy, and Gino-coauthored.

convergent_concepts.concept: Depth is less awkward than you fear
convergent_concepts.agreement: People underestimate how welcome deep and sensitive questions are; questions about values, turning points and stories build connection.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: David Brooks pushes big crossroads questions; Duhigg stresses light, reciprocal deep questions; Wood Brooks offers a graduated pyramid and says not every conversation needs to go deep.

convergent_concepts.concept: Social fears and self-perceptions are miscalibrated
convergent_concepts.agreement: People overestimate awkwardness and how much others notice their stumbles, underestimate the positive impact of depth, compliments and vulnerability, and overestimate how clearly their tone comes across. Stage 3 sources add independent lab and field evidence: new acquaintances like us more than we think, lapsed contacts welcome a hello more than we expect, a declined invitation stings less than feared, assertive people rarely cross the line they fear crossing, nerves are less visible than they feel, speakers overestimate how often they were understood, and email readers infer more urgency than senders intend.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Some books use the finding to encourage action (Wood Brooks, David Brooks, Madson, Abrahams); others to urge verification (Schramm, Duhigg on text). Several papers come from one lab and some links are mapped rather than cited. The added papers come from several independent labs (Cornell, Chicago, Columbia, Virginia Tech), which strengthens the convergence, though most measure beliefs and forecasts rather than what happens when people act on corrected beliefs.

convergent_concepts.concept: Ask rather than infer other minds
convergent_concepts.agreement: You know less about others' thoughts, feelings and intentions than you believe; ask and check rather than assume. Meta-analytic research adds that lie detection from behavior is barely above chance and that nonverbal cues are weak, probabilistic hints, so asking and listening beat watching.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: David Brooks's mentalizing model projects from your own experience and Wood Brooks's compass asks for a best guess at partner goals, which sit uneasily with perspective-getting research. how-to-know-a-person-06 is not confirmed in the book.

convergent_concepts.concept: Looping and paraphrasing for understanding
convergent_concepts.agreement: Restate what you heard in your own words and check; it catches misunderstanding and lowers defensiveness. Keysar and Henly add the speaker side: ask the listener for their version rather than trusting a nod.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Duhigg and David Brooks describe the full loop; Brooks allows a lighter paraphrase; Abrahams also uses paraphrase to buy time and reframe hostile questions; Schramm applies verification to writing. Some research finds paraphrase adds little over acknowledgment.

convergent_concepts.concept: Connection over perfection
convergent_concepts.agreement: Aim for adequate rather than impressive, treat mistakes as offers, recover lightly and keep going.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Madson frames it as life philosophy; Abrahams adapts it from Madson and limits it to in-the-moment delivery; Schramm frames it as long-run mastery; Aaker and Bagdonas apply it to humor. Lineage reduces independence.

convergent_concepts.concept: Reframe anxiety rather than suppress it
convergent_concepts.agreement: Manage nerves to a workable level and redirect arousal rather than trying to eliminate it. Research sources add arousal reappraisal and stress mindsets (treat the racing heart as fuel), distanced self-talk, and knowing that nerves are less visible than they feel.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Abrahams calms the body first, then relabels and reframes; Schramm adds power posing, which failed to replicate; Madson says act while nervous rather than fixing feelings first. The excitement effect replicated on feelings more than on performance. Jamieson frames the goal as a challenge rather than threat response, not as excitement; Bodie adds that skills training is itself an anxiety treatment when the fear comes from feeling unprepared.

convergent_concepts.concept: Reusable message structures (What, So What, Now What and relatives)
convergent_concepts.agreement: A short reusable shape eases delivery under pressure and helps listeners follow; good structures end with relevance and a next step.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Abrahams uses What So What Now What for spontaneous speech, Schramm for written synthesis; Madson prefers questions-to-self over scripts; Wood Brooks and Duhigg offer conversation structures rather than message structures. None is tested as a named framework.

convergent_concepts.concept: Lead with the core point and cut the preamble
convergent_concepts.agreement: Find the single most important point, say it first, and drop background the audience does not need. Minto's pyramid puts the governing point first, and field experiments from Rogers and Lasky-Fink show that cutting whole ideas, not only words, raises response rates.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Made to Stick stresses ruthless prioritization; Schramm stresses opening at the most engaging moment; Abrahams stresses relevance and concision; Madson's start with the obvious is about not waiting for brilliance.

convergent_concepts.concept: Curse of knowledge and audience-first planning
convergent_concepts.agreement: Start from what the audience knows, cares about and must do; your own sense of clarity is unreliable.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Schramm orders the work (AIM, canvas); Made to Stick diagnoses the cause and prescribes stickiness tools; Abrahams compresses it to an in-the-moment check; Madson and Wood Brooks focus on purpose and goals. Key curse-of-knowledge studies are unpublished or replicated at smaller size.

convergent_concepts.concept: Disclosure and vulnerability build trust when reciprocal and calibrated
convergent_concepts.agreement: Sharing feelings and uncertainties, reciprocated, deepens relationships; disclosure should not undermine core competence.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Connect prescribes gradual 15 percent steps with the higher-status person first; Duhigg says vulnerability often precedes trust; Schramm emphasizes purpose for an audience; David Brooks counsels patience; Aaker and Bagdonas add laughter as an accelerant.

convergent_concepts.concept: Match the kind of conversation before responding
convergent_concepts.agreement: Misfires often come from people being in different conversations; diagnose what the other person needs and meet them there.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Duhigg uses three kinds plus mood and energy; Wood Brooks uses a goals compass and five layers; David Brooks distinguishes official and actual conversations; Connect and David Brooks apply it to support. All typologies are untested syntheses.

convergent_concepts.concept: Feedback: behavior and impact, not motive or personality
convergent_concepts.agreement: Name specific observable behavior and its effect, avoid labels and intent guesses, and ask for behavior change rather than character change.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Connect treats feedback as data, not a verdict, and rejects the sandwich; Abrahams adds explicit Implications; Schramm adds coaching and Radical Candor.

convergent_concepts.concept: A learning stance in disagreement
convergent_concepts.agreement: Aim to understand rather than win: acknowledge the other view, find the real layer of difference and points of agreement, and treat the exchange as joint problem solving.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Wood Brooks gives a linguistic receptiveness recipe; Abrahams's CLEAR starts with self-regulation; Duhigg measures success by feeling heard; David Brooks stresses safety before content. Key receptiveness papers are Gino-coauthored, with independent support from Ren and Schaumberg.

convergent_concepts.concept: Humor: lightness over jokes, with asymmetric risk
convergent_concepts.agreement: Humor is mainly a mindset; successful humor signals confidence, mild flops cost little, inappropriate humor costs a lot; laughing at others' humor counts.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Aaker and Bagdonas argue humor is underused and give craft and safety checks; Wood Brooks favors low-risk levity; Madson frames play as loosening the mind; Duhigg treats laughter as a signal to match. Two books share one research paper.

convergent_concepts.concept: Make stories and specifics do the work
convergent_concepts.agreement: Concrete details, examples, analogies, human-scale numbers and short stories improve understanding and memory. Meta-analyses confirm that stories persuade, mainly by absorbing the listener (transportation), and field experiments show that exchanging personal stories shifts entrenched views where arguments alone do not.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Made to Stick is the theoretical anchor; Schramm offers a story template (Low); Abrahams embeds a concrete example in each structure; David Brooks applies it to listening by asking for others' stories. Stories-versus-statistics figures are informal. Braddock and Dillard put the size in perspective: narrative effects are small (correlations around .2), so stories nudge rather than convert.

convergent_concepts.concept: Persuade through the listener's benefit
convergent_concepts.agreement: Start from a problem the listener recognizes, help them picture their benefit, and close with a clear ask.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Made to Stick adds non-material motives and self-imagery; Abrahams and Schramm package pitch structures; Duhigg distinguishes cost-benefit from similarity logic by conversation type.

convergent_concepts.concept: Identity shapes what people hear
convergent_concepts.agreement: Messages are processed through identity; threats to identity harden resistance, while shared or valued identities open people up. Moral reframing research shows that arguing from the listener's values, not your own, moves people across political lines.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Made to Stick uses identity as a persuasion lever; Duhigg uses it to defuse resistance and set norms; Wood Brooks treats it as a layer of difference; Schramm applies it to the speaker's own identity (Low).

convergent_concepts.concept: Apologize specifically and own it
convergent_concepts.agreement: Name the specific act and its effect, avoid 'but' and conditional apologies, commit to change; ruptures can be repaired. Lewicki and colleagues rank the parts: plainly accepting responsibility matters most and offering repair second, while asking for forgiveness adds least.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Abrahams gives a three-part form; Wood Brooks adds superfluous apologies for others' bad luck; Aaker and Bagdonas apply it to jokes that cross a line; Connect describes the long arc of repair.

convergent_concepts.concept: Express appreciation more than feels necessary
convergent_concepts.agreement: Specific thanks and sincere compliments are undergiven and land better than expected. Relationship research adds that responding with enthusiasm to good news and a steady supply of small positives keep relationships resilient, and that unprompted check-ins are appreciated more than senders expect.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Wood Brooks frames it as a miscalibration; Madson as a Naikan reflection habit; Abrahams builds thanks into toasts; Duhigg prescribes extra gratitude online.

convergent_concepts.concept: Raise small issues early and make expectations explicit
convergent_concepts.agreement: Unspoken irritations and mismatched expectations accumulate; raise them early in non-accusatory language and set norms explicitly. Managing-up and friendship sources apply the same rule upward and to friends, and couples research finds direct requests for change work better than hinting when the problem is serious.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Connect supplies the core models; Abrahams stresses in-the-moment timing; Duhigg applies norm-setting to groups. Mostly one book.

convergent_concepts.concept: Elevate others in groups
convergent_concepts.agreement: Make partners look good, build on offers, ask rather than dominate, and laugh at others' humor; dominance lowers shared understanding.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Madson grounds it in improv ethics, Duhigg in neural-alignment research, Aaker and Bagdonas in status-aware leadership humor, David Brooks in the midwife model.

convergent_concepts.concept: Presence and inquiry before advice when someone is struggling
convergent_concepts.agreement: Resist fixing; ask open questions, acknowledge how hard it is, and stay present. Research on person-centered comforting (23 studies) and on support that misfires supports acknowledging and legitimizing feelings before offering advice, and offering advice with permission when it is wanted.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: David Brooks addresses clinical depression and pairs presence with professional care; Connect addresses everyday problems; Duhigg frames it as matching an emotional conversation. Key cases are single anecdotes. Rafaeli and Gleason add that support the person notices can backfire, so less visible support sometimes helps more, which sits in tension with naming feelings explicitly.

convergent_concepts.concept: Practice, record and reflect
convergent_concepts.agreement: Skills improve through feedback-driven practice: debriefs, recordings, rehearsal with a partner, frequent small feedback. Randomized trials of structured speaking practice programs give this the strongest evidence in the library.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Schramm gives the most developed routines; Abrahams prescribes drills; Wood Brooks uses TALK as a checklist; Connect frames feedback as data you cannot get yourself.

convergent_concepts.concept: Know when to move on or end
convergent_concepts.agreement: People stay too long on stale topics and in conversations; switch or close warmly and exit together.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Wood Brooks supplies evidence and warning signs; Abrahams supplies an exit technique.

convergent_concepts.concept: Pushing hardens resistance: draw out their reasons and listen
convergent_concepts.agreement: When someone is dug in, more arguments tend to strengthen their defense of the status quo. Asking for their own reasons, listening without judging, offering choices and exchanging stories lower defensiveness and leave room for them to move themselves.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Motivational interviewing is a clinical method tested in trials; Kalla and Broockman tested door-to-door conversations; the listening experiments come mostly from one lab; Berger and Fisher and Ury are practitioner syntheses. Effects per conversation are small, so the realistic goal is a modest shift, not a conversion.

convergent_concepts.concept: Interests over positions, and the pie is rarely fixed
convergent_concepts.agreement: Look beneath stated positions to the needs that drive them, assume there may be issues where both sides want the same thing or value things differently, and invent and trade across options before bargaining.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Fisher and Ury give a practitioner method; Thompson grounds it in experiments on fixed-pie and lose-lose errors; Cohen and Bradford apply exchange to colleagues you cannot direct. Duhigg and Wood Brooks extend the idea to everyday conversation.

convergent_concepts.concept: Reciprocity and exchange drive influence without authority
convergent_concepts.agreement: People repay what they receive, so giving first, in a currency the other person values, builds the goodwill that later requests draw on, with peers, bosses and contacts alike.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Cialdini stresses personal, unexpected gifts; Cohen and Bradford a deliberate trade; King giving without keeping score. The door-in-the-face meta-analysis warns that a concession-driven yes often fails to become action.

convergent_concepts.concept: Busy readers: fewer ideas, one ask, visible structure
convergent_concepts.agreement: Readers decide quickly whether and how deeply to engage, so cut whole ideas, make one easy request, and mark the few things that matter with consistent headings or emphasis.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Rogers and Lasky-Fink test messages in the field; the signaling meta-analysis comes from learning materials; Minto and Schramm are practitioner methods. Over-formatting backfires, so emphasis must stay scarce.

convergent_concepts.concept: Good meetings are designed, not just run
convergent_concepts.agreement: Most of a meeting's quality is decided by purpose, invitations, agenda, time and process, and leaders overrate their own meetings. How a group collaborates predicts performance more than who is in it.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: The meeting-science sources share authors and a research community, so this is partly lineage; Riedl's collective intelligence evidence is independent. Camera norms are supported by one field experiment.

convergent_concepts.concept: In close relationships, be direct about problems but gentle with the person
convergent_concepts.agreement: Name a specific behavior and the change you need instead of attacking character, hinting or inducing guilt; raise it while it is small.
convergent_concepts.disagreement: Gottman stresses a gentle start-up; Overall and McNulty find that direct opposition, even with visible frustration, produces change when the problem is serious and the partner can change, and harms when it is minor.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: A research-based or well-documented practitioner source on asynchronous and remote written work: writing for decisions, documentation culture, response-time norms, channel choice. Candidates to evaluate: books on digital workplace communication (for example Erica Dhawan's Digital Body Language, Cal Newport's A World Without Email) and organizational research on email and chat norms.
gaps.status_note: Response-time norms, writing for busy readers and channel choice are now covered with research; documentation culture remains thin.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: A structured-memo method (for example Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle) and a research-based guide to writing for busy readers (for example Rogers and Lasky-Fink's Writing for Busy Readers). Current coverage is one unconfirmed insight and one secondary tag.
Same sources as proposals-memos; only two books contribute and none is writing-focused.
Peer-reviewed research on video-call communication and fatigue plus a practitioner guide to virtual presenting; the only insight is Low and not confirmed in the book.
gaps.status_note: Video-fatigue research now covers hosting and attending; no practitioner source on presenting virtually was added.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: Same as public-speaking/virtual; the three tagged insights are Low, unconfirmed or tangential.
gaps.status_note: Both Medium: one theory paper with a large correlational follow-up and one field experiment.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: An assertiveness and refusal source (for example William Ury's The Power of a Positive No) and research on refusals and request compliance; only connect-13 touches it, framed as boundaries.

A research-based persuasion source covering reciprocity (for example Cialdini's Influence) and Cohen and Bradford's Influence Without Authority, already mentioned in Stage 1 under connect-12. The only tagged insight is about compliments.
Research or practitioner guidance on introducing yourself, introducing others and following up; neither tagged insight is about introductions as such.
gaps.status_note: Following up after first meetings and having others introduce your credentials are covered; no source teaches introducing yourself or others as such.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: Research-based bad-news delivery protocols (for example the clinical SPIKES literature) and organizational research on communicating layoffs and change; no current insight gives a delivery sequence.
gaps.status_note: Organizational layoff and change communication is still not covered.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: An assertiveness or boundaries source grounded in research; coverage is two Connect insights and one humor caveat.
Research on social support and peer support for people in distress or grief; one of three insights rests on a single personal case.
A friendship-research source; two of seven tagged insights are Low and none has friendship as its primary category.
A family and parenting communication source (for example Faber and Mazlish) and guidance on conversations with aging parents; all family tags are secondary.
gaps.status_note: Family is covered through relationship research applied to family members; no parenting source was added, and conversations with aging parents remain a documented unfilled gap by user decision.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: A couples-research source (for example Gottman's work, currently only mapped in Stage 1 rationales); all partner tags are secondary applications.
A research-grounded negotiation text (for example Getting to Yes or a negotiation research textbook); no current source is negotiation-focused.
A research-based treatment of nonverbal communication that corrects myths (Mehrabian misapplication, power posing, voice pitch); current items are contested or anecdotal.
gaps.status_note: Power posing is addressed through a supporting-evidence entry from the Korner meta-analysis rather than a separate insight.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: Research on meeting effectiveness (for example Rogelberg's The Surprising Science of Meetings); 23 tags but none about running meetings.
A source on project and status communication for managers; three secondary tags only.
gaps.status_note: Documented unfilled gap by user decision. gabarro-kotter-managing-your-boss-03 (no surprises) and mroz-allen-2018-meetings-01 touch it as secondary tags only.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: A dedicated Q and A or media-training source; one of four tagged insights is Low and unconfirmed and one is contested.
Framing research beyond Made to Stick; two books contribute and the identifiable-victim anchor failed a pre-registered replication.

An independent review of humor-at-work research to balance Humor, Seriously, which supplies 16 of 19 humor insights and whose authors have an incentive to stress benefits; five humor insights are Low.
gaps.status_note: One independent meta-analysis now balances Humor, Seriously, but its evidence is correlational.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: Narrative persuasion research and a confirmed story-structure source; two of eight insights are Low and the story spine is unconfirmed in the book.
gaps.status_note: All three High; the story spine remains unconfirmed.

gaps.what_would_fill_it: Research-based guidance on conversations with aging parents (driving, health decisions, care arrangements).
gaps.status_note: Documented unfilled gap by user decision; no thin insight was written to fill it.
